_comment: Story beats shown after action completion. Conditions (all optional): dayMin, dayMax, wisdomMin, wisdomMax, langMin, langMax, contactsMin, contactsMax, spiritDryMin, spiritDryMax, npcMet (string), stageMin_{npcId}, stageMax_{npcId}, moodMin/Max_{npcId}, stressMin/Max_{npcId}, burdenMin/Max_{npcId}, daysNotSeenMin_{npcId}. Empty conditions = catch-all fallback. Optional `rewards` object overrides the action's blanket non-trust rewards (NPC trust always comes from action def). Optional `penalty` object deducts stats AFTER rewards: penalty.faith/wisdom/contacts use positive magnitudes (subtract); penalty.trust is { id, amount } (subtract trust, never past current stage floor); penalty.spiritDry is a signed delta; penalty.npcMood/npcStress/npcBurden are signed deltas as { id, amount }.

pray.text: You kneel on the tatami mat. The city bleeds through the thin walls — bicycle bells, a distant train announcement in Japanese you can't parse. Your prayer comes in English, instinctively. '神様...' you start, then trail off into your own language. You figure God can translate.

You're finding a rhythm. Morning prayer feels like something you're earning — not just reciting. You pray by name for the people you've met, for the ones who took a tract and kept walking, for the old man on the bench.

After a month, prayer feels less like a discipline and more like breathing. You've started to understand why Japanese Christians talk about prayer as 静まること — stillness. Not performance. Just presence.
You pray for Kenji today — for whatever he's carrying that he won't name. You don't know enough yet to pray specifically. You just hold him before God and trust that's enough.
You pray for Hiro. For Emiko. For whatever it means that he comes to that bench every morning, facing the same direction, watching the same pigeons. That kind of faithfulness deserves a name.
Your mind goes everywhere but where you want it. You drag it back, again and again. A half-hour later you're not sure much happened. But you stayed. Maybe that's the whole thing.
The words come, but feel like they're landing on the ceiling. You finish anyway. Sometimes prayer is just showing up when you don't feel like it.
You pray. The words feel unfamiliar in this place, but the intention isn't.
You sit. Nothing comes. You stay anyway. The room is very quiet and you are not sure what you are doing here. You stay until the timer goes off.

rest.text: You sleep without dreaming. Wake up still tired. The clock ticks on regardless.
You rest. The neighbors are quiet for once. You wake up feeling like a person again.

study_scripture.text: You read slowly. Verses that felt clear back home carry new weight here. 'Go into all the world.' You're in it now — this particular corner of it, with its particular silences. You underline more than usual.

You find yourself reading through the lens of everything you've seen. The parable of the sower. The soil here isn't harder than anywhere else — just different. You're starting to understand the difference. That feels like progress.
Something in Paul's letter to the Romans catches in a way it never has before. You read it three times, slowly. Write it out by hand. The city outside makes different sense through this lens.

The Word is becoming your anchor. You've started marking verses that specifically apply to what you see in Tokyo — in the salary-worker exhaustion, in the crowds that flow past without eye contact. The Gospel was written for exactly this.
Your eyes keep sliding off the page. You read the same verse four times. Closed the Bible. Sat. Opened it again. You're not sure you absorbed much. But you didn't stop.
You open the Bible and read until something lands. Today, something does.
The words slide off. You read the same paragraph four times before giving up. You wonder if you forgot how to do this.

study_japanese.text: Hiragana first. Forty-six characters before you can read a children's book. You trace each one slowly — あ、い、う、え、お — like learning to walk again. The notebook is filling up. You are a beginner. You are okay with that.

You can read the station signs now. Small victory. You practice the phrases that matter: すみません (excuse me), ありがとうございます (thank you). A man at the convenience store actually understood your order in Japanese today. He looked surprised. So did you.

You're starting to hear the shape of sentences — where the verb goes, how politeness is layered into grammar itself. Japanese is a language where what you don't say matters as much as what you do. That's a sermon in itself.
One more hour. One more page. The language is coming, slowly.
You drag through flashcards. Your brain feels like wet cardboard. You're not absorbing anything. You finish the set anyway because you said you would.

hand_tracts.text: Most people don't take one. Some bow politely and keep walking. A few accept it without slowing down. One woman looks at the cover — a cross above the Tokyo skyline — and her expression is unreadable. The tract does the talking. You can't yet.

You try saying すみません as you hand them out. It helps. People are more surprised that you speak any Japanese than they are by the tract itself. A teenager actually laughs — not meanly — and takes one. Progress.
Your approach is smoother now. You can read hesitation, adjust your timing. A woman in her 40s takes a tract, reads the title quietly to herself: 神の愛. God's love. She doesn't hand it back.
Every suit that rushes past reminds you of Kenji. You wonder what he thought when he took that first tract. Whether he still has it.
Another handful distributed. You don't know what happens to them after. That's okay. You didn't plant the trees you're sitting under.
Someone tears the tract in your face and drops it at your feet. They keep walking. You stand there a moment before bending to pick it up.
Kenji passes you in the rush. You're sure he saw — you're sure he didn't. He keeps walking. You hand the next tract to a stranger.

commuter_convo.text: You catch a man reading an English novel on the train and ask about it — English first, then a word of Japanese. He brightens. 'My Japanese must be terrible,' you say. He shakes his head politely: 'No, no — very good.' He's being kind. You'll take it.

You manage a full exchange with a woman commuting to work. She asks why you're in Japan. You tell her the truth. She doesn't flinch. 'That is unusual,' she says. 'For Tokyo.' You agree. She seems to find that interesting.
A student asks about Christianity — curious, not skeptical. You explain simply. He listens all the way to his stop, then bows and thanks you. 考えてみます. I'll think about it. That's all you asked for.
Brief connection made in transit. Sometimes a seed is a sentence.
You try a phrase. The man stares at you, then turns away. The carriage feels louder for a moment, then exactly the same as before.

open_air_preach.text: You speak in English. A small cluster forms — mostly younger people curious about the foreigner. You watch their faces more than you hear your own words. Most move on after a minute. One stays the whole time and then applauds. You bow, not sure what else to do.

You mix languages now — English foundation, Japanese phrases where you know them. The crowd is small but steadier. A father stops with his daughter. She tugs his sleeve and asks him something. He shrugs — then stays.

Preaching in Japanese is still imperfect, but it's real. An elderly woman listens the whole time. Afterward she says something you don't fully catch — but you hear the word 祈り. Prayer. You bow back and thank her.
You think of Hiro watching from his bench as you preach. You wonder if anyone preached here twenty years ago, when his wife was still alive. Whether she ever stopped to listen.
Three people took a tract. Two dropped it immediately. One man stopped briefly, then hurried on. Some days are like this. You pack up and head home.
A group of salarymen walks past, one muttering something dismissive. You finish the message to the empty plaza. It takes more out of you than a successful day ever does. You go home tired.
The park echoes differently each time. Today a few people stopped. That's enough.
A passerby films you on his phone, laughing. Two teenagers walk by mocking your accent. You finish anyway. You're not sure who that was for.
The words come out, but feel hollow even to you. No one stops. You don't blame them.

casual_convo.text: Smiles and nods carry a lot — you learn this early. A grandmother on the bench offers you a piece of mochi from her bag. You accept. She doesn't speak English, you barely speak Japanese, but the gesture is perfect.

You can introduce yourself now — name, where you're from, what you're doing in Japan. The reaction is usually the same: raised eyebrows, then a slow smile. A missionary? In Tokyo? They thought those were something from another century.

A longer conversation today — about family, about why you came. The man you spoke with lost his job last year. He comes to the park to think. Something in your words catches. He asks if you'll be here again. You will.
Small talk in a foreign language is its own kind of courage.
You try to start a conversation with an older man on the bench. He smiles politely, says something in Japanese, then opens his newspaper. You sit a while longer just so leaving isn't embarrassing.

host_english.text: Eight people came. Three stayed the full session. You taught vocabulary, answered questions about American culture, and somewhere in the middle someone asked about church. You didn't force it. You just answered honestly. The room got quieter — in a good way.

The conversation went beyond language tonight. A student asked why English feels 'more open' than Japanese — why it's easier to say certain things. You told her that in English you have to put the self first. In Japanese the self disappears into context. She wrote that down.
You scan the room for Yuki's face when you set up. She's usually early. Tonight she brought a friend from her department who 'just wanted to see what this was.' That's how it starts.
Language is just the door. You're always hoping they'll come inside.
Only one person shows up. He's polite but quiet. You drink coffee with him for an hour and he leaves early. You take the chairs down by yourself.

observe_shrine.text: You watch without judgment. People pass through — some hurried, some careful. An older woman claps twice, bows, and stands in silence for a long moment. You don't know what she's asking for. But you recognize the posture.

You're beginning to understand the pull this place has. Not as a rival to what you believe, but as a window into what people long for: cleansing, connection, an ear that listens. The form is different. The longing isn't.

You think of Hiro here. He says he's not religious — but he comes to the park every day, faces the same direction, sits in the same spot. Everyone is worshipping something. Most people just don't call it that.
You sit and observe. You're starting to see.
You bow the wrong number of times. A priest gently corrects you in front of the gathered visitors. Your face burns. You finish the visit but leave faster than you planned.

onsen_visit.text: You weren't sure what to expect. There's a ritual to it — the washing first, the specific movements, the quiet. Nobody talks much. An older man nods at you across the steam. You nod back. Something passes between you that language couldn't have carried.

You got into a real conversation — in the changing room, of all places. A man about your age, between jobs, thinking about what comes next. You talked for twenty minutes. The steam relaxes people. Walls come down. You think about what that means for the Gospel.
You mentioned the onsen to Kenji once. He laughed: 温泉は日本人の教会だ. Onsen are the church of the Japanese. He meant it as a joke. You didn't entirely take it that way.
The onsen strips away pretense. Something about that always opens doors.
You stay longer than usual. The steam hides your face. You leave feeling lighter — not whole, but reachable again.

visit_kenji.text: You find the coffee kiosk near Gate 3. Kenji arrives on time, suit pressed, phone in hand. You pull out your own phone — Google Translate. He watches you type. He types back. The exchange is slow and clumsy and occasionally wrong. But he doesn't check his watch. When you stand up to leave he bows precisely and says something you don't catch. You bow back. That's enough for now.

You meet Kenji at the station coffee kiosk. Your Japanese is enough for the basics now — you can ask about his work, say something about the weather, thank him properly. He loosens slightly. He tells you the name of his company. Small thing. But he offered it; you didn't ask. That's the difference.

You meet Kenji for coffee near the station. He's formal — same suit he always wears. He asks about your family, your hometown, your church back home. He listens carefully and gives careful answers. You learn he has a younger sister. That's more than he's told anyone at work in years.

Kenji meets you at the kiosk but barely touches his coffee. He holds his phone and types: '会社が... restructuring.' You look up the word. Restructuring. He stares at the cup. You don't know how to say what you'd want to say. You sit with him anyway. He stays longer than usual.

Kenji is quieter than usual. He says one word — 大変, 'difficult' — and looks away. You ask if it's work. He nods slowly. His coffee sits untouched. You don't push. You've learned that silence with Kenji isn't empty — it's how he processes things. He comes back next week.

Kenji is quieter than usual. His company announced restructuring. He says it without emotion, like reading a train schedule. But his coffee sits untouched for ten minutes. You don't rush to fill the silence. He eventually says: 'I don't know what I'm working for.' You wait. He doesn't say more. But he comes back next week.

Kenji types a question into his phone and holds it up: 'Do you really believe all this?' You read it. You type back: 'Yes.' He reads your answer several times. He doesn't respond. But there's something in his face that wasn't there before.

Kenji asks slowly, choosing each word: 'Is it... okay, to doubt? In your faith?' You tell him yes — that doubt and faith aren't opposites. He repeats the word in Japanese: 疑い. Doubt. He seems to be filing it somewhere.

The questions are different now. Kenji wants to know about doubt — whether real faith allows for it. You tell him that doubt and faith are not opposites. He looks like you said something slightly illegal. Then he almost smiles.

Kenji arrives looking hollow. His coffee goes cold. At some point he says: 'I don't know how people do this for twenty years.' He means the job. Maybe more. You stay until he has to leave. He thanks you before he goes — more carefully than usual.

Kenji is running on nothing. He's been at the office until midnight three days this week — he mentions it like it's weather. You ask what he does to rest. He thinks for a long time. 'Sleep,' he says. 'Sometimes.' You don't push. You make sure he finishes the coffee.

He mentions the restructuring as fact, not complaint. Department cut by a third. Not him — not this time. But the way he says it means he knows he's on borrowed time. He's been through this before. His father never came home from the 1998 restructuring either.
He asks out of nowhere: 'Do you ever feel like the life you're living is the wrong one?' He doesn't mean the job. You both know that. You take your time answering. He doesn't check his phone once.
He's there, but he's somewhere else. He apologizes twice for things that don't need an apology. At some point he says: '最近ちょっと...' — Lately a little... — and trails off. You nod. You stay.
It's been a while. He says so before you sit down, almost like an apology. 'I thought maybe you had given up on me.' You tell him you haven't. He nods once and picks up his coffee.

Something is lighter in him today. He's the one who suggests the coffee place, which almost never happens. He asks about your week and actually listens. He laughs once — briefly, genuinely — at something you say. You notice it because it's rare.
You and Kenji meet. It matters more each time.
He's polite but he checks his watch four times. The conversation never lands. You leave feeling like you took up his time more than you spent it with him.
Something is wrong and you can't ask. The silence sits heavy. He finishes his coffee. He bows. He goes.

visit_yuki.text: Yuki is waiting with her notebook open. She's written out her questions in English — careful, complete sentences. She leads the whole conversation. You answer in English; she takes notes. The dynamic is slightly backwards from what you'd expect. She seems to find your situation genuinely interesting, like a linguistics puzzle she hasn't seen before.

Yuki comes with questions in her notebook as usual. But today you answer one in Japanese — halting, imperfect. She stops writing and looks up. 'Your Japanese,' she says, 'you're really studying.' The way she says it isn't polite surprise. It's actual respect. Language is her world. Effort in it means something.

Yuki comes with a list of questions she wrote out in a notebook. She's looked up theological terms in English and Japanese. She wants to know if Christianity is compatible with Japanese culture. You answer each question honestly. She writes down your answers. The conversation runs twenty minutes past when she said she had to leave.

Yuki seems different today — lighter. She types something and shows you her phone: a church near her apartment. 'I went,' she types. 'Just to see.' She watches your face carefully. You smile. She seems relieved, though you're not sure why she expected anything else.

Yuki tells you quietly that she visited a church near her apartment. 'I didn't tell you,' she says carefully in Japanese. 'In case I didn't like it.' She pauses. 'I liked it.' She looks uncertain — like she's not sure what that means yet. You tell her that's okay. She writes something in her notebook.

She admits she's been going to church — just to see. Not yours. A church near her apartment. 'I didn't want you to know yet,' she says, 'in case I didn't like it.' She liked it. She's not sure what to do with that.

Yuki slides her phone across — she's been reading John chapter 1 in Japanese and English side by side, highlighting phrases. She points to one: 言葉は神であった. The Word was God. Then: 言葉は肉体となった. The Word became flesh. She types: 'Why flesh? Why not just a message?' You sit with that. It's exactly the right question.

Yuki has been reading John's prologue. She asks slowly: 'Why did God... become a person? Why not... send a letter?' It comes out partly in Japanese, partly in English. Either way the question is precise. You tell her: because a message can be ignored. A person cannot. She writes that down.

Yuki has been reading the Gospel of John in Japanese and English side by side. She has questions about the prologue — 'In the beginning was the Word.' She thinks she understands now why the Word had to become flesh. Why God couldn't just send a message. You sit with that. 'I've never heard it put that way,' you tell her. 'It's exactly right.'

Yuki comes with too many books and too little sleep. She's been studying for something — she mentions it and moves on quickly. Her questions today are faster, more fragmented. She's working something out under the surface. When you ask if she's okay she says 'I'm fine' and immediately asks something she clearly wrote out last night.

She's unusually still when you arrive — not the usual cascade of notes and questions. She tells you she tried praying last week. 'I didn't know if I was doing it right.' You tell her you still don't fully know. She seems relieved by that.

She says she went to her grandmother's grave last Saturday. She brought incense — she doesn't believe in it the way her grandmother did, but she brought it anyway. 'I didn't know how else to show up.' You tell her that showing up counts. She thinks about that for a moment, then writes something in her notebook.

She's there when you arrive but her notebook stays closed. She lets you talk more than usual. Whatever is pressing on her, she's not ready to name it yet — and you don't push. Sometimes just showing up is the answer to a question that hasn't been asked yet.

Yuki had sent one short LINE message — 忙しいです, I'm busy — and then nothing. When you finally meet, she seems both glad and slightly guilty. She doesn't say it, but you can tell she wondered if you'd stop making the effort. You stayed. That matters to her.
Yuki asks good questions. You're both figuring something out.
She closes her notebook early. 'I have to study,' she says. You're not sure that's true. You don't ask.

visit_hiro.text: You get two cans of coffee from the vending machine and sit beside him. He accepts his without looking at you. The pigeons come and go. You don't understand most of what he says — you catch 奥さん, wife, and 毎日, every day. You nod. He keeps talking anyway, softly, more to himself than to you. Sometimes that's enough.

You bring coffee from the vending machine. Hiro accepts it and speaks slowly — he's patient with your Japanese, more than most people. He tells you her name. Emiko. Just once. He looks at the pigeons after. You don't push. You've learned not to push with Hiro.

You bring two cans of coffee from the vending machine. Hiro accepts his without looking at you. You sit beside him. The pigeons circle. He tells you about his wife — her name was Emiko, she liked chrysanthemums, she used to get up before dawn to pray. He doesn't say what she prayed to. He doesn't have to.

Hiro asks you something slowly. You catch only part of it — 死んだ人、聞こえる？ The dead... hear? You look it up on your phone. He watches you read. When you look up, you say yes — you believe so. He nods once and looks back at the pigeons. That nod means something.

Hiro asks today, carefully: 'Dead people... can they hear us?' You tell him you believe so — not because you can prove it, but because you trust it. He sits with that for a long time. Then quietly: 'Emiko would have liked you.' You don't say anything. Some things don't need a response.

Hiro asks you today: 'Do you think the dead can hear us?' You pause. He's not asking academically. You tell him you believe so — not from proof, but from faith. He sits with that for a long time. 'Emiko would have liked you,' he says finally. That undoes you a little.

Hiro reaches into his jacket and brings out a small Bible — worn, marked with paper strips. He opens to a page and reads aloud very slowly. You don't understand every word. But you recognize the cadence. Someone underlined that verse a long time ago. He closes it carefully and looks at the pigeons.

Hiro brings Emiko's Bible to the bench today. He opens it to a bookmarked page. 'She marked this,' he says simply. He reads it aloud. Your Japanese is just good enough to follow. Afterward he says nothing. You say nothing. The park is very quiet.

Hiro tells you he started reading the Bible Emiko kept in the bedside drawer. He found her bookmarks inside — she had underlined things. He reads you one of them aloud, slowly. His voice doesn't shake. He's past the stage where it does.
He doesn't look up right away. You buy two coffees anyway and sit. When you stand to leave he says quietly: ありがとう. He means it fully.

Today he doesn't want to talk. You can feel it immediately. You buy two coffees and sit. He accepts his without comment. At some point he says: 'Emiko used to sit with me like this. Not talking. Just there.' He doesn't say anything after that. You stay anyway.
Hiro is waiting when you arrive — he's been watching the path. He wants to talk. You can tell. He just needs you to be the one who starts. You sit. You ask. He begins.

A quiet morning. The grief is still there — it doesn't leave — but today it seems to sit lighter. He tells you about the neighborhood where he and Emiko used to live before the kids were born. He doesn't usually talk about before. Today he does.
He doesn't say he noticed your absence — he wouldn't — but when you sit down he turns toward you more fully than usual. The pigeons gather close. Some things don't need to be said.
You sit with Hiro. Some visits don't need many words.
He's there. He looks up when you sit down — slowly. He doesn't say anything for a long time. You feel the distance you let grow. You'll have to start showing up again.

evening_kenji.text: Two hours at the café. Most of it is through phone translation — slow and imperfect. But something still happens. He types about his father: 父は... disappeared. He looks up from the screen. You type back: 'Mine too, in a different way.' He reads it carefully. You sit in that for a while. Some things translate.

Kenji talks for almost two hours. He uses simple words — he's patient with you, and you with him. His father worked until he vanished from the family without dying. His mother prayed at the altar every morning. He says: 'I don't understand... how to believe something.' You tell him: that might be the beginning. He writes that down in his phone.

Two hours over ramen. Kenji talks about his father — a man who worked until he disappeared from the family without dying. A mother who prayed at the altar every morning for a husband who had already left in every way that mattered. 'I don't know how to believe in anything,' he says. You tell him that might be exactly the right place to start.
A long time at the café. Half translation app, half silence, half something you don't have a word for. Kenji stays the whole time. That's not nothing.
A long conversation with Kenji. Not everything landed perfectly — but enough did. The kind of conversation you come away from changed, even if you can't say exactly how.

Kenji says less than usual but what he says lands harder. 'I think I'm disappearing,' he says at one point — slowly, like he's testing the words. 'Into the job. Into the schedule.' He asks if you've ever felt like that. You tell him yes — that faith helps you locate where you actually are. He's quiet for a long time. He writes something in his phone.

He asks you something he's been sitting with: whether a person can believe something they can't prove. Not as a debate. As a genuine question about his own life. You talk for a long time. When he finally looks up, it's gotten dark outside.

This conversation is the most unguarded he's ever been. He asks about conversion — what it actually means, whether it's a decision or something that happens to you. He's not asking abstractly. You take your time. He doesn't check his phone once. That's the measure of how present he is.
A long conversation with Kenji. The kind that changes things.

questions_yuki.text: Yuki types and talks and shows you things in her notebook for almost two hours. At one point she cries a little — you catch the word 家族, family — and keeps going like it didn't happen. You don't know all of what she said. But you know something came out that had been held in for a long time.

Yuki tells you she's afraid to believe — not because it isn't true, but because of her family. She's an only child. Her grandmother burned incense every morning. 'Is that... wrong?' she asks carefully. You tell her: loving the dead is not wrong. She sits with that. Her eyes are wet. She doesn't apologize for it.

Yuki tells you she's been afraid to believe — not because she thinks it's untrue, but because of what her parents would think. She's an only child. Her grandmother burned incense for her grandfather every morning. 'Is that wrong?' she asks. You tell her that loving the dead is not wrong. That love doesn't have to be opposed to faith. She cries a little. You're not sorry it came out.
A long café conversation, mostly in English with her leading. Something real passed between you anyway. That's becoming a pattern with Yuki.
A long conversation with Yuki. You followed more than you expected. She's close to something — you can feel it even when you can't always say the right words.
A long conversation with Yuki. She's closer than she knows.
She asks a careful question. You hear the word for soul — 魂 — but the rest gets away from you. Your answer comes out wrong. She nods politely. She doesn't write it down.

pray_hiro.text: Hiro gestures at you — pray. He folds his hands loosely, the way he's seen you do it. You pray out loud, in English, slowly. He closes his eyes. The park is quiet. When you finish he sits for a long time. Then one sentence, soft: something about Emiko. You catch her name. That's enough.

Hiro asks you to pray — in Japanese, if you can. You try. It comes out rough. He keeps his eyes closed the whole time. When you finish he says quietly: 'Emiko wa... so prayed.' His voice stays level. He's practiced this particular stillness for a long time.

Hiro asks you to pray — out loud, in whatever language you like. He closes his eyes while you do. When you finish he sits quietly for a while. 'I think she prayed like that,' he says. 'Emiko.' He doesn't say anything after that. Neither do you. The silence is not empty.
A long time on the bench together. Mostly quiet. That's how it works with Hiro — the length of the silence is a kind of language.
Time with Hiro. Something between you that doesn't fully need words. Something is growing.
He doesn't look up right away. You buy two coffees anyway and sit. The pigeons come and go. When you stand to leave he says quietly: ありがとう. He means it fully.

Today he doesn't want to talk. You can feel it immediately. You buy two coffees and sit. He accepts his without comment. At some point he says: 'Emiko used to sit with me like this. Not talking. Just there.' He doesn't say anything after that. You stay anyway.

Hiro is waiting when you arrive, which is new — he's usually there first but today he's been watching the path, waiting for you. He wants to talk. You can tell. He just needs you to be the one who starts. You sit. You ask. He begins.

He's on the bench when you arrive but not feeding the pigeons. Just sitting. You buy coffee and put one in his hand. He says 'The thirty-first' — nothing else. You don't ask what happened on the thirty-first. You stay the whole time.

A quiet morning. The grief is still there — it doesn't leave — but today it seems to sit lighter. He tells you about the neighborhood where he and Emiko used to live before the kids were born. He doesn't usually talk about before. Today he does.

He's on his usual bench. He doesn't say he noticed your absence — he wouldn't — but when you sit down he turns toward you more fully than usual. The pigeons gather close. Some things don't need to be said.
Time with Hiro. Something is growing.
